text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, good news for parents of children with asthma. Dyslexia
in a digital world. The media and cancer reporting. And a caution for people with
high blood pressure. Don't ignore the bottom number of your pressure, what's
called your diastolic.

Last November on the Health Report we covered a study called the SPRINT trial
which found that for people at high risk of a heart attack or stroke, going on to
high blood pressure treatment which aimed for a top number or systolic blood
pressure of 120 or less was associated with significant benefits compared to the
usual target of 140. This has made many countries wonder whether they should
tell doctors to lower blood pressure targets in their patients at high risk of heart
disease.

But you'll notice I have only talked about the top number, the systolic pressure
which is the pressure generated by the heart beating and pumping blood through
your arteries. The bottom number, the diastolic pressure, is the background
pressure between heartbeats and has a critical role in keeping blood going to
organs like the brain and heart. A group led by researchers at Johns Hopkins
University in Baltimore was concerned that there might be a risk in people whose
diastolic pressure falls too far with more aggressive blood pressure treatment. It's
a story consumers need to know about. Bill McEvoy was the lead author, and I
spoke to him earlier today.

Bill McEvoy: Patients who have very stiff blood vessels, which is a risk factor for
heart disease and stroke, the diastolic pressure, which is the pressure you have
between heartbeats, tends to be lower. And that means that there can be less
profusion of the organ during diastole, which is for all intents and purposes
approximately half of the heartbeat.

Norman Swan: And just to capture what you said there, essentially a low
diastolic blood pressure could be a reflection of very stiff arteries in somebody
who is already considerably at risk.

Bill McEvoy: Yes, and to add to that, most patients with stiff arteries tend to
have higher systolic blood pressures, and that means that the pulse pressure,
which is the difference between the two, systolic minus diastolic, is larger. So
 
those patients with a higher pulse pressure, which is the higher systolic and the
lower diastolic, might be due to stiff arteries. If they are going to be treated to this
target of 120, they may end up with a non-treatment diastolic blood pressure that
is lower than we would like and that has theoretical reasons for concern,
specifically with respect to the coronary blood flow.

The coronary arteries, as you know, are the arteries that supply the heart muscle
itself, and those coronary arteries, because they go through the heart muscle,
when that the heart squeezes in cystoid, which is the time when the heart is
pumping blood out, those vessels are constricted and there is no flow. So the
only time that there is actually flow to the heart muscle through those coronary
arteries is during diastole, and for that particular reason it could be that in
diastole when the diastolic blood pressure is too low that you are getting actually
reduced blood flow to the heart muscle which can cause damage.

Norman Swan: So you studied 11,500 people, average age 57, both men and
women, to look at the relationship between whether or not you could measure
heart damage by a chemical called troponin, related to their diastolic blood
pressure. Were those people being treated for their blood pressure or this was
their natural diastolic blood pressure?

Bill McEvoy: It was a mix. This was a fairly healthy population in their 50s, and
specifically did not have a prior history of coronary artery disease. So most of the
patients were not on treatments. We found that even when we stratified the
analysis based on hypertension treatment status, that is we looked both at the
group of patients or adults in the study who were getting treatment for blood
pressure and we looked at the group who were not on any treatment, we saw
that the results were the same. That is, that the diastolic blood pressure, the
lower that blood pressure was, the more likely that we saw an association with
heart damage by this troponin.

Norman Swan: What's the significance of that raised troponin? Was it high
enough to be registered as a heart attack or is it just chronic damage that could
lead to heart failure, for example?

Bill McEvoy: More the latter than the former. We know from prior studies that
individuals with troponin levels this high are far more likely to have adverse
 
outcomes, specifically adverse coronary heart disease, cardiac death and most
particularly adverse heart failure outcomes. So I see this as individuals who are
ambulating, walking around their communities, likely mostly asymptomatic, who
have detectable levels of heart muscle injury relating to the lower diastolic blood
pressure and the consequent reduction in the coronary blood flow. And again,
our take-home message is that the SPRINT study is important, there are
individuals who will benefit from a lower systolic blood pressure, I think that can't
be underestimated, but a real simple point in this analysis was that physicians
really need to look at both.

Norman Swan: And you're cut-off that you thought was the one that was
significant was 70, that the bottom number shouldn't fall below 70.

Bill McEvoy: Yes, we certainly saw a trend for certain outcomes for heart
disease and for the troponin outcome we saw a significantly elevated association
in the individuals who have diastolic blood pressure less than 70, and particularly
less than 60 would be of concern.

Norman Swan: So what's a general practitioner to do, because you can't treat
diastolic by itself, you've only got one blood pressure pill or one lifestyle measure,
what are you to do?

Bill McEvoy: I think in an individual who for instance has an elevated systolic
blood pressure and in whom the general practitioner is considering blood
pressure treatment, I think they need to assess what the diastolic blood pressure
is, understand that particularly for patients who have known coronary artery
disease, who have had prior bypass surgery, prior heart attacks, that particularly
in those individuals who have that history who have a wide pulse pressure, I think
there needs to be some caution in pushing the systolic blood pressure too low.

Norman Swan: But the SPRINT people would say, well, we did a randomised
controlled trial and we properly studied it in a randomised way, all you've done is
looked at a group of people, which is not as good evidence.

Bill McEvoy: So they haven't reported the outcomes based on diastolic blood
pressure, so I would say that's an average result, and therefore it's fair to say that
on average if you take a given patient and take them at random and you treat
them, if they have the criteria for SPRINT to a systolic of 120, they are likely
 
going to benefit. But for the individual who has a low diastolic blood pressure I
would advocate that those patients not be treated as aggressively, particularly if
they have a history of coronary artery disease. I think this is just something that
puts a little bit more emphasis on the individual rather than on the average. It
doesn't contradict the SPRINT study in any way, it just really highlights the point
that diastolic blood pressure shouldn't be ignored and that for individuals who
start off with that low diastolic blood pressure there needs to be some caution of
dropping it lower, particularly if they have known coronary artery disease.

Norman Swan: Bill McEvoy, thanks for joining us on the Health Report.

Bill McEvoy: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Bill McEvoy is in the cardiology department at Johns Hopkins
University School of Medicine in Baltimore.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, at ABC News Radio and
CBC Radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

25 or 30 years ago Australia had the dubious record of having just about the
highest death rates from asthma in the world. No one knew quite why, but it was
thought in part because people were overusing their reliever inhalers,
medications like Ventolin, and not using their preventers, which are usually
inhaled steroids which actually treat the underlying disease. Ventolin is a short-
acting member of a family of medications called beta-agonists which allow the
airways to relax. In the last few years drug companies have produced long-acting
beta-agonists which only need to be taken once or twice a day. It is known that
these long-acting drugs should not be used by themselves but in combination
with inhaled steroids they have conquered the market for asthma medications,
yet no one has been absolutely sure they are safe, even in combination. But last
week a large trial in children was published trying to answer that question, and it
follows a similar study in adults. Someone with a close interest in this is
Professor Christine Jenkins who is head of respiratory trials at the George
Institute in Sydney. Welcome to the Health Report.

Christine Jenkins: Thank you Norman.

Norman Swan: So what did this study in children find?
 
Christine Jenkins: This study is, as you said, a very large study. In fact it was
designed to look at the safety of long-acting beta-agonists in combination with
inhaled corticosteroids. So the long-acting beta-agonist is not being given alone
here, it is being given in the single inhaler with an anti-inflammatory medication,
versus that anti-inflammatory medication alone. This was a six-month study in
children aged between four and 11, and they looked at what we call the severe
asthma related events, and those events were either episodes where children
had attacks so that they needed to take an oral corticosteroid, a course of
prednisolone, or even worse, might have been admitted to hospital, for instance.
And a severe asthma event of course also includes a death from asthma.

But most importantly there were no deaths from asthma in this study, and in fact
there was a very, very low rate, fewer than 2% of the children actually had severe
asthma related events over this six-month period. And what it showed was there
was no difference in these outcomes between the children who took the inhaled
steroid only, that is the anti-inflammatory only, and those who took the
combination long-acting beta-agonists with anti-inflammatory. So this was a very
reassuring study in terms of the safety of these medications. But further to that, it
also showed in fact that the benefits of the long-acting beta-agonist with the
inhaled corticosteroid were equal if not slightly superior to the benefits of the anti-
inflammatory alone. So a very productive study on both counts.

Norman Swan: But it didn't look as if it was worth actually adding the LABA to it
because there wasn't that much difference between the two. You might as well
just have the child on the steroid alone.

Christine Jenkins: It's true, and indeed most children should only be treated
with inhaled corticosteroids alone. In fact, most children don't even need
continuous anti-inflammatory medication. So that's an important thing to say
about this study, it actually recruited children who had had a hospital admission
or severe asthma related event requiring corticosteroids in the previous 12
months. So we are already including a group of children who are at slightly
higher risk of these events. And indeed, those children are at the more severe
end of the spectrum who might need continuous medication. Most children in
Australia don't need continuous anti-inflammatory medication for their asthma
because they have mild, intermittent episodes.
 
Norman Swan: So earlier on in the year there was a study in adults, what did
that show? That was about 11,000 adults.

Christine Jenkins: Exactly. So these are very large studies because they are
safety studies. Most studies of medications in respiratory medicine at least, and I
think it's true for most other disciplines, are looking for the benefits of the
treatment, and you don't need nearly as many people in a trial looking for
benefits when you know a drug is efficacious than you do in a trial where you are
looking for much less frequent events such as adverse events related to the
potential danger of the drug.

So these studies had to be by nature very large, and this was an 11,000-person
study, a multicentre study conducted globally. And what it showed too in adults
was that the long-acting beta-agonist combined with the anti-inflammatory steroid
was superior in efficacy and not inferior in safety in any respect, both in adults
and children.

Norman Swan: So when you say superior in efficacy, the adult one showed that
there was an added benefit from adding the long-acting beta-agonist.

Christine Jenkins: Correct, in reducing the number of asthma episodes
requiring courses of oral corticosteroid, yes.

Norman Swan: These were the Glaxo drugs. There's two competing drugs here,
there's Astra who produce one set of this combination and there's Glaxo, and
they have been in fierce competition for years. So Glaxo has funded these trials.
Is it going to apply to the Astra drug which is the one that a lot of GPs would be
prescribing?

Christine Jenkins: Well, that's a very good question. In fact these trials were
mandated by the Food and Drug Authority in the US to address this question of
safety. There has been what's called a black box, black label warning on the
packaging of these medications in the US, and that has been because there
were much earlier some studies which were observational studies primarily that
suggested that long-acting beta-agonists might be dangerous.

This is a problem in the US particularly where people might take these two drugs
in separate inhalers and end up only taking the long-acting beta-agonist. The
 
very point you made in your introduction is that beta-agonists alone as a
maintenance treatment for asthma are not safe and should not be taken without
an anti-inflammatory. But this is a situation that has happened in the US
particularly because the medications are very expensive, and people often
default to the treatment that works for them…

Norman Swan: But you haven't answered my question about which is better, the
Astra preparation or the Glaxo one, or can you apply what was found from the
Glaxo study to the Astra medication?

Christine Jenkins: Yes, apologies, my long-winded preamble was to tell you
that the FDA mandated that all the manufacturers of these drugs conducted
these studies. So these are the Glaxo SmithKline studies, and AstraZeneca has
also published a study also this week in the New England Journal of
Medicine demonstrating in adults the safety of their preparation in exactly the
same way in adults, and indeed showing that not only are they safe and not
inferior to the anti-inflammatory alone, they are superior in efficacy. And the
Novartis company, which also manufactures these drugs, is still undertaking the
tail end of their studies, and they will be published too. So we will know across
the board for this whole class of medications from each of these studies.

Norman Swan: Chris Jenkins, thanks for joining us.

Christine Jenkins: Thanks very much Norman.

Norman Swan: Professor Christine Jenkins, head of respiratory trials at the
George Institute in Sydney.

Last week the Lancet published a paper from the UK which on the face of it was
quite disturbing in terms of the 30-day death rates and people starting anti-
cancer treatment for breast and lung cancer. According to cancer researcher
Darren Saunders, what may be more interesting than the paper is how the media
reported it. Darren works at the University of New South Wales. Welcome to
the Health Report Darren.

Darren Saunders: Hi Norman.

Norman Swan: What did the study show?
 
Darren Saunders: The study is quite interesting actually. They took all of the
data from the NHS for patients that had had treatment for breast cancer or lung
cancer in 2014, so it's almost 30,000 patients. And they looked at mortality within
a month of their last line of chemotherapy basically, and found that there were
some factors that predetermined which people would respond and which people
would die from those chemotherapies. That's not necessarily surprising, the
shock was how it was reported, more than anything else.

Norman Swan: And just briefly, what people were at most risk? Was it any
surprise?

Darren Saunders: Not really, things like age, people with lung cancer that were
already smokers, so people that were more frail tended not to respond so well to
chemotherapy, which is not that surprising.

Norman Swan: And people obviously with palliative chemotherapy.

Darren Saunders: People with palliative did worse. And there was some grainy
differences between the different hospitals.

Norman Swan: And there were differences between the hospitals which people
should take note of. So how was it reported?

Darren Saunders: The two main reports, one was in the Telegraph in the UK,
one was in the Guardian, and both got picked up on social media.
The Telegraph splashed with…their lead paragraph was all about chemotherapy
killing half the patients that get it. And that's…not anywhere in the paper does it
say that. And I've been through the press releases that went with it and nowhere
in those press releases do they say that.

Norman Swan: Okay, I guess it's a good headline.

Darren Saunders: Yes, and that got, as you could imagine, amplified massively
on social media, and I saw some really disturbing responses from patients and
patients' families saying, well, that's convinced me, I've told my doctor I don't
want therapy. The study didn't compare how people went with or without therapy,
so people are making big decisions based on this reporting here.

Norman Swan: And the Guardian?
 
Darren Saunders: The Guardian got it better, they actually pretty much covered
the story well. It was less sensationalist. They made some important points, but
they did it much better.

Norman Swan: And the argument here of course is because it goes out on
social media it washes against our shores as well. So was there much evidence
that it washed against our shores?

Darren Saunders: It did, it was widely reported even by some science and
health reporters within Australia on social media unfortunately.

Norman Swan: Picking up on the Telegraph headline rather than
the Guardian headline.

Darren Saunders: Yes, exactly, that was the headline that was quoted.

Norman Swan: So it's literally viral, it's infectious.

Darren Saunders: So it brings up this notion of…and forgive my language here,
this notion of the unbearable asymmetry of bullshit, as Brian Earp, the
philosopher in the UK has called it, and that's this notion that the amount of
energy necessary to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than it is to
produce it in the first place.

Norman Swan: How does this affect people like you who are cancer
researchers?

Darren Saunders: Frustration is the first word I'd use, it's incredibly frustrating.
It's hard enough getting accurate information out to people in the first place, and
when it's…I wouldn't say deliberately misrepresented but obviously not well
reported, it gets most of us pretty upset actually, to be honest.

Norman Swan: What's the poor punter to do? We had the Catalyst on statins
which reduced…some people would say cost 2,000 lives in Australia over a
period of time because people at high risk went off their statins. What is the poor
punter to do to actually work out what is a reliable article versus an unreliable
article?
 
Darren Saunders: It's really hard, especially when the by-line is science editor of
the Telegraph, that should be coming from a reputable voice. I guess I normally
point patients towards the National Institutes of Health in America or Cancer
Research UK or the Cancer Institute New South Wales who have reputable, well
collated information.

Norman Swan: So double-check before you decide that it's going to affect your
therapy.

Darren Saunders: Definitely.

Norman Swan: And this falls hard on the heels of bacon killing half the
population.

Darren Saunders: That was a great example…

Norman Swan: Cured meats and cancer.

Darren Saunders: Yes, the BBC reported that as being equally risky as
asbestos and plutonium, which it's clearly not.

Norman Swan: Yes, it smells too good for that! Darren, thanks for joining us.

Darren Saunders: Thanks Norman.

Norman Swan: Darren Saunders, who is in the department of pathology at the
University of New South Wales, and gnashing his teeth over cancer research
reporting.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on Radio National.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, depending on the state that you
live in, up to 50% of the population of Australia are functionally illiterate. A
proportion of these people will have dyslexia, but that's far from the only reason.
This Saturday, Learning Difficulties Australia's 2016 Eminent Researcher Award
is to be given to an old friend of the Health Report, Professor Maryanne Wolf,
who is director of the Centre for Reading and Language Research at Tufts
University in Boston, and she has dragged herself into the studio. Welcome back
Maryanne.
 
Maryanne Wolf: It's a pleasure to be back. Of course I have a multifactorial
response to give you and it's a developmental one, so pardon me if I give you
four different reasons at four different ages. The first is 0 to 5. We know that the
gaps really begin before the children even walk in the kindergarten door. So what
we could do to enhance language development is so simple, literally reading to
our children, speaking to our children every day, every night, is one of the
simplest antidotes to really the very grievous differences in language in our
privileged and underprivileged homes.

Norman Swan: So this is the notorious word gap.

Maryanne Wolf: This is the notorious word gap in which 32 million less words
are heard by children who are between three and four who come from
disadvantaged homes. And it's not just quantitative, it's qualitative as well, you
know, the nature of the language that is being used. But yes, that's the first, the 0
to 5.

Norman Swan: But if you've got 50% of the population, I think that's a
Tasmanian figure actually, I think it's less in other states, but if you've got a
large…even 30% is high, and their parents, they are going to struggle to read to
their children.

Maryanne Wolf: Absolutely. There are wonderful things that we can do, and part
of it is due to the paediatricians who are giving these various groups of children
stories that can be read either by the people who are the parents or by librarians
or by caretakers or by tape recorders…

Norman Swan: This is the US context.

Maryanne Wolf: This is the US context and it's called Reach Out and Read. But
any group can do this. So there's all kinds of ways we can do that. But actually I
think the more pernicious factor is happening between kindergarten and grades
two and three, and that's…and Norman, we've spoken about this before. I see a
certain recidivism going on in Australia in our methods of teaching children. So
regardless…

Norman Swan: So this is not the first time you've been to Australia?
 
Maryanne Wolf: This is definitely not the first time, I've even spoken to you
Norman about things that will make people very upset, and that is the nature of
instruction that goes on to children who come from whatever home they are…

Norman Swan: So this is before we even get on to dyslexia.

Maryanne Wolf: Oh, well before.

Norman Swan: And what you're talking about here is teachers training colleges
not teaching teachers evidence-based literacy.

Maryanne Wolf: Exactly. What I really was…I was so hopeful about Australia but
I see a retreat to binary modes of instruction…

Norman Swan: So what do you see happening?

Maryanne Wolf: I see instead of us really reflecting the research on evidence-
based instruction and the…

Norman Swan: And I should say there are like 30 randomised control trials of
this, this is not…

Maryanne Wolf: Yes, this is nothing new.

Norman Swan: And what we're talking about here, just to cut to the chase, is the
evidence-based teaching is phonics, sounding out words, understanding the
science within words and relating them to the written text, amongst other things.

Maryanne Wolf: Okay, amongst other things. But the way that I want the whole
public to understand this is that phonics provides the first scaffolding of a reading
brain circuitry. But by no means do people who have all the good intent in the
world in teaching whole language, we don't leave them behind, we provide that
scaffolding and expand it…

Norman Swan: And for those people who are listening to this for the first time,
whole language is the notion that there is something natural about reading. Your
point is that it's very unnatural to learn, that we didn't evolve to read. And they
think just by showing text and telling nice stories, kids will get it. And some kids
will, but not all.
 
Maryanne Wolf: Yes, right. Between 50% and 60% any method works, but for
the rest of our children we are literally not giving them the lower rungs of the
ladder. So they will never in fact reach their potential as truly expert readers
because of this.

Norman Swan: I'm used to hammering doctors for not being evidence-based,
now we are hammering teachers. What evidence have you got that there is
recidivism amongst Australian teachers and they are contributing to this
unacceptably high level of illiteracy?

Maryanne Wolf: What I have been doing for the last week but also for the last
several months is really trying to understand from teachers, policymakers,
administrators, what is going on, and what seems to be is a regression to a kind
of binary way of thinking about instruction.

Norman Swan: Binary?

Maryanne Wolf: Binary being phonics versus whole language and we can call it
balance but it's not balance. And what we really need to do is to understand
evidence base gives us a scaffolding. It also helps all children who have various
forms of impairments. So dyslexia is between 5% and 10% of the population.
There are many other challenges. But if you give this scaffolding and then you
expand it…you see, the reading brain circuit is not simply about phonics, that's
the beginning. I need teachers to realise they need to be explicit about everything
over time. So we are talking about rich semantic or vocabulary work…

Norman Swan: So it's understanding the world and the context for the written
word…

Maryanne Wolf: Exactly, syntax, the grammar, there's so much that is beautiful
about this reading brain circuit that is literally being taught in one way or another
versus a developmental sequenced way of bringing it all together.

Norman Swan: So do you think primary school teachers understand that syntax
and the grammar?

Maryanne Wolf: No, they do not. One of the really harsh realities is that primary
teachers are given the responsibility for all the ills the society is not addressing.
 
They are given 20, 25 or 30 children, they were never trained to work with
children with dyslexia or challenges, and they are giving usually one hour a week
from someone outside and no pull-out time for the children who need intensive
work.

Norman Swan: We're going to run out of time, so very briefly, looking at the 5%
of kids with dyslexia…

Maryanne Wolf: 5% to 10%, yes.

Norman Swan: I've been on a campaign about this with teachers, training
colleges, and obviously failed miserably. All we can do is talk about it. But I'm not
talking about the 5% who've got dyslexia and really something neurological going
on in their brain, what is new there in terms of being able to help them?

Maryanne Wolf: One of the most exciting aspects of all this work in
neuroscience is that we understand that our previous conceptualisation of
dyslexia was all wrong. It's not about a deficit or a defect, it's about a difference
in the brain organisation of those children. The educational system has not
understood that it is not the child, it's us. We can learn to teach this by
understanding how the reading brain circuit works and addressing each
component. That takes training. But we have evidence trials right now going on
from NICHD, we have wonderful methods that can with intensive pull-out training,
small group, we can do so much good, and release the potential of some of our
most creative minds who are dyslexic.

Norman Swan: So is handing an iPad to a baby changing the reading pathway?

Maryanne Wolf: Goodness gracious, the iPad is the new pacifier with the same
problems…

Norman Swan: Seriously, is the digital world changing how…?

Maryanne Wolf: The fourth factor I would say in functional illiteracy is the fact
that the digital world is in fact changing attention, especially in the young brain,
which is very susceptible. So you have addiction problems, you have children
who are literally developing a reading brain circuit that is short circuited, that
 
doesn't have the advantages because it's moving its attention sometimes 27
times an hour, they are not developing concentration…

Norman Swan: So you're talking about video-based material with rapid
intercutting.

Maryanne Wolf: But there's so many aspects to the digital culture that are
changing us. They are changing attention, memory, reliance on external
platforms of knowledge rather than building inside the children an internal…

Norman Swan: Most parents would think they are giving their children this
deeper knowledge and exposure to the world through the digital environment.
What is a parent to do?

Maryanne Wolf: First of all there's some wonderful work done by different
people, and what I would really suggest is that we have a developmental model.
Under two, I want no iPads. Between two and five, very gradual. At 5 to 7 I want
only use of the digital work in school for coding and programming. And then over
time, then we gradually use it, ever gradually.

Norman Swan: So it's not a tool for learning to read?

Maryanne Wolf: It is a tool that could be used carefully and critically. Literally we
need scales of justice here Norman, and in one minute I'm not going to be able to
say this but I will say that what I hope is a bi-literate brain that is critically able to
use and know when to use a digital reading and when to use print at what
developmental period. So it's a bi-literate brain over time developmentally taught.

Norman Swan: And Maryanne Wolf has got a couple of books coming out on
that which we will no doubt promote when they do. Maryanne, thanks very much
for joining us again on the Health Report.

Maryanne Wolf: Of course!

Norman Swan: Maryanne Wolf is director of the Centre for Reading and
Language Research at Tufts University in Boston.

I'm Norman Swan and you've been listening to the Health Report. I do hope you
can join us again next week

Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, good news for parents of children with asthma. Dyslexia
in a digital world. The media and cancer reporting. And a caution for people with
high blood pressure. Don't ignore the bottom number of your pressure, what's
called your diastolic.

Last November on the Health Report we covered a study called the SPRINT trial
which found that for people at high risk of a heart attack or stroke, going on to
high blood pressure treatment which aimed for a top number or systolic blood
pressure of 120 or less was associated with significant benefits compared to the
usual target of 140. This has made many countries wonder whether they should
tell doctors to lower blood pressure targets in their patients at high risk of heart
disease.

But you'll notice I have only talked about the top number, the systolic pressure
which is the pressure generated by the heart beating and pumping blood through
your arteries. The bottom number, the diastolic pressure, is the background
pressure between heartbeats and has a critical role in keeping blood going to
organs like the brain and heart. A group led by researchers at Johns Hopkins
University in Baltimore was concerned that there might be a risk in people whose
diastolic pressure falls too far with more aggressive blood pressure treatment. It's
a story consumers need to know about. Bill McEvoy was the lead author, and I
spoke to him earlier today.

Bill McEvoy: Patients who have very stiff blood vessels, which is a risk factor for
heart disease and stroke, the diastolic pressure, which is the pressure you have
between heartbeats, tends to be lower. And that means that there can be less
profusion of the organ during diastole, which is for all intents and purposes
approximately half of the heartbeat.

Norman Swan: And just to capture what you said there, essentially a low
diastolic blood pressure could be a reflection of very stiff arteries in somebody
who is already considerably at risk.

Bill McEvoy: Yes, and to add to that, most patients with stiff arteries tend to
have higher systolic blood pressures, and that means that the pulse pressure,
which is the difference between the two, systolic minus diastolic, is larger. So

those patients with a higher pulse pressure, which is the higher systolic and the
lower diastolic, might be due to stiff arteries. If they are going to be treated to this
target of 120, they may end up with a non-treatment diastolic blood pressure that
is lower than we would like and that has theoretical reasons for concern,
specifically with respect to the coronary blood flow.

The coronary arteries, as you know, are the arteries that supply the heart muscle
itself, and those coronary arteries, because they go through the heart muscle,
when that the heart squeezes in cystoid, which is the time when the heart is
pumping blood out, those vessels are constricted and there is no flow. So the
only time that there is actually flow to the heart muscle through those coronary
arteries is during diastole, and for that particular reason it could be that in
diastole when the diastolic blood pressure is too low that you are getting actually
reduced blood flow to the heart muscle which can cause damage.

Norman Swan: So you studied 11,500 people, average age 57, both men and
women, to look at the relationship between whether or not you could measure
heart damage by a chemical called troponin, related to their diastolic blood
pressure. Were those people being treated for their blood pressure or this was
their natural diastolic blood pressure?

Bill McEvoy: It was a mix. This was a fairly healthy population in their 50s, and
specifically did not have a prior history of coronary artery disease. So most of the
patients were not on treatments. We found that even when we stratified the
analysis based on hypertension treatment status, that is we looked both at the
group of patients or adults in the study who were getting treatment for blood
pressure and we looked at the group who were not on any treatment, we saw
that the results were the same. That is, that the diastolic blood pressure, the
lower that blood pressure was, the more likely that we saw an association with
heart damage by this troponin.

Norman Swan: What's the significance of that raised troponin? Was it high
enough to be registered as a heart attack or is it just chronic damage that could
lead to heart failure, for example?

Bill McEvoy: More the latter than the former. We know from prior studies that
individuals with troponin levels this high are far more likely to have adverse

outcomes, specifically adverse coronary heart disease, cardiac death and most
particularly adverse heart failure outcomes. So I see this as individuals who are
ambulating, walking around their communities, likely mostly asymptomatic, who
have detectable levels of heart muscle injury relating to the lower diastolic blood
pressure and the consequent reduction in the coronary blood flow. And again,
our take-home message is that the SPRINT study is important, there are
individuals who will benefit from a lower systolic blood pressure, I think that can't
be underestimated, but a real simple point in this analysis was that physicians
really need to look at both.

Norman Swan: And you're cut-off that you thought was the one that was
significant was 70, that the bottom number shouldn't fall below 70.

Bill McEvoy: Yes, we certainly saw a trend for certain outcomes for heart
disease and for the troponin outcome we saw a significantly elevated association
in the individuals who have diastolic blood pressure less than 70, and particularly
less than 60 would be of concern.

Norman Swan: So what's a general practitioner to do, because you can't treat
diastolic by itself, you've only got one blood pressure pill or one lifestyle measure,
what are you to do?

Bill McEvoy: I think in an individual who for instance has an elevated systolic
blood pressure and in whom the general practitioner is considering blood
pressure treatment, I think they need to assess what the diastolic blood pressure
is, understand that particularly for patients who have known coronary artery
disease, who have had prior bypass surgery, prior heart attacks, that particularly
in those individuals who have that history who have a wide pulse pressure, I think
there needs to be some caution in pushing the systolic blood pressure too low.

Norman Swan: But the SPRINT people would say, well, we did a randomised
controlled trial and we properly studied it in a randomised way, all you've done is
looked at a group of people, which is not as good evidence.

Bill McEvoy: So they haven't reported the outcomes based on diastolic blood
pressure, so I would say that's an average result, and therefore it's fair to say that
on average if you take a given patient and take them at random and you treat
them, if they have the criteria for SPRINT to a systolic of 120, they are likely

going to benefit. But for the individual who has a low diastolic blood pressure I
would advocate that those patients not be treated as aggressively, particularly if
they have a history of coronary artery disease. I think this is just something that
puts a little bit more emphasis on the individual rather than on the average. It
doesn't contradict the SPRINT study in any way, it just really highlights the point
that diastolic blood pressure shouldn't be ignored and that for individuals who
start off with that low diastolic blood pressure there needs to be some caution of
dropping it lower, particularly if they have known coronary artery disease.

Norman Swan: Bill McEvoy, thanks for joining us on the Health Report.

Bill McEvoy: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Bill McEvoy is in the cardiology department at Johns Hopkins
University School of Medicine in Baltimore.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN, at ABC News Radio and
CBC Radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

25 or 30 years ago Australia had the dubious record of having just about the
highest death rates from asthma in the world. No one knew quite why, but it was
thought in part because people were overusing their reliever inhalers,
medications like Ventolin, and not using their preventers, which are usually
inhaled steroids which actually treat the underlying disease. Ventolin is a short-
acting member of a family of medications called beta-agonists which allow the
airways to relax. In the last few years drug companies have produced long-acting
beta-agonists which only need to be taken once or twice a day. It is known that
these long-acting drugs should not be used by themselves but in combination
with inhaled steroids they have conquered the market for asthma medications,
yet no one has been absolutely sure they are safe, even in combination. But last
week a large trial in children was published trying to answer that question, and it
follows a similar study in adults. Someone with a close interest in this is
Professor Christine Jenkins who is head of respiratory trials at the George
Institute in Sydney. Welcome to the Health Report.

Christine Jenkins: Thank you Norman.

Norman Swan: So what did this study in children find?

Christine Jenkins: This study is, as you said, a very large study. In fact it was
designed to look at the safety of long-acting beta-agonists in combination with
inhaled corticosteroids. So the long-acting beta-agonist is not being given alone
here, it is being given in the single inhaler with an anti-inflammatory medication,
versus that anti-inflammatory medication alone. This was a six-month study in
children aged between four and 11, and they looked at what we call the severe
asthma related events, and those events were either episodes where children
had attacks so that they needed to take an oral corticosteroid, a course of
prednisolone, or even worse, might have been admitted to hospital, for instance.
And a severe asthma event of course also includes a death from asthma.

But most importantly there were no deaths from asthma in this study, and in fact
there was a very, very low rate, fewer than 2% of the children actually had severe
asthma related events over this six-month period. And what it showed was there
was no difference in these outcomes between the children who took the inhaled
steroid only, that is the anti-inflammatory only, and those who took the
combination long-acting beta-agonists with anti-inflammatory. So this was a very
reassuring study in terms of the safety of these medications. But further to that, it
also showed in fact that the benefits of the long-acting beta-agonist with the
inhaled corticosteroid were equal if not slightly superior to the benefits of the anti-
inflammatory alone. So a very productive study on both counts.

Norman Swan: But it didn't look as if it was worth actually adding the LABA to it
because there wasn't that much difference between the two. You might as well
just have the child on the steroid alone.

Christine Jenkins: It's true, and indeed most children should only be treated
with inhaled corticosteroids alone. In fact, most children don't even need
continuous anti-inflammatory medication. So that's an important thing to say
about this study, it actually recruited children who had had a hospital admission
or severe asthma related event requiring corticosteroids in the previous 12
months. So we are already including a group of children who are at slightly
higher risk of these events. And indeed, those children are at the more severe
end of the spectrum who might need continuous medication. Most children in
Australia don't need continuous anti-inflammatory medication for their asthma
because they have mild, intermittent episodes.

Norman Swan: So earlier on in the year there was a study in adults, what did
that show? That was about 11,000 adults.

Christine Jenkins: Exactly. So these are very large studies because they are
safety studies. Most studies of medications in respiratory medicine at least, and I
think it's true for most other disciplines, are looking for the benefits of the
treatment, and you don't need nearly as many people in a trial looking for
benefits when you know a drug is efficacious than you do in a trial where you are
looking for much less frequent events such as adverse events related to the
potential danger of the drug.

So these studies had to be by nature very large, and this was an 11,000-person
study, a multicentre study conducted globally. And what it showed too in adults
was that the long-acting beta-agonist combined with the anti-inflammatory steroid
was superior in efficacy and not inferior in safety in any respect, both in adults
and children.

Norman Swan: So when you say superior in efficacy, the adult one showed that
there was an added benefit from adding the long-acting beta-agonist.

Christine Jenkins: Correct, in reducing the number of asthma episodes
requiring courses of oral corticosteroid, yes.

Norman Swan: These were the Glaxo drugs. There's two competing drugs here,
there's Astra who produce one set of this combination and there's Glaxo, and
they have been in fierce competition for years. So Glaxo has funded these trials.
Is it going to apply to the Astra drug which is the one that a lot of GPs would be
prescribing?

Christine Jenkins: Well, that's a very good question. In fact these trials were
mandated by the Food and Drug Authority in the US to address this question of
safety. There has been what's called a black box, black label warning on the
packaging of these medications in the US, and that has been because there
were much earlier some studies which were observational studies primarily that
suggested that long-acting beta-agonists might be dangerous.

This is a problem in the US particularly where people might take these two drugs
in separate inhalers and end up only taking the long-acting beta-agonist. The

very point you made in your introduction is that beta-agonists alone as a
maintenance treatment for asthma are not safe and should not be taken without
an anti-inflammatory. But this is a situation that has happened in the US
particularly because the medications are very expensive, and people often
default to the treatment that works for them…

Norman Swan: But you haven't answered my question about which is better, the
Astra preparation or the Glaxo one, or can you apply what was found from the
Glaxo study to the Astra medication?

Christine Jenkins: Yes, apologies, my long-winded preamble was to tell you
that the FDA mandated that all the manufacturers of these drugs conducted
these studies. So these are the Glaxo SmithKline studies, and AstraZeneca has
also published a study also this week in the New England Journal of
Medicine demonstrating in adults the safety of their preparation in exactly the
same way in adults, and indeed showing that not only are they safe and not
inferior to the anti-inflammatory alone, they are superior in efficacy. And the
Novartis company, which also manufactures these drugs, is still undertaking the
tail end of their studies, and they will be published too. So we will know across
the board for this whole class of medications from each of these studies.

Norman Swan: Chris Jenkins, thanks for joining us.

Christine Jenkins: Thanks very much Norman.

Norman Swan: Professor Christine Jenkins, head of respiratory trials at the
George Institute in Sydney.

Last week the Lancet published a paper from the UK which on the face of it was
quite disturbing in terms of the 30-day death rates and people starting anti-
cancer treatment for breast and lung cancer. According to cancer researcher
Darren Saunders, what may be more interesting than the paper is how the media
reported it. Darren works at the University of New South Wales. Welcome to
the Health Report Darren.

Darren Saunders: Hi Norman.

Norman Swan: What did the study show?

Darren Saunders: The study is quite interesting actually. They took all of the
data from the NHS for patients that had had treatment for breast cancer or lung
cancer in 2014, so it's almost 30,000 patients. And they looked at mortality within
a month of their last line of chemotherapy basically, and found that there were
some factors that predetermined which people would respond and which people
would die from those chemotherapies. That's not necessarily surprising, the
shock was how it was reported, more than anything else.

Norman Swan: And just briefly, what people were at most risk? Was it any
surprise?

Darren Saunders: Not really, things like age, people with lung cancer that were
already smokers, so people that were more frail tended not to respond so well to
chemotherapy, which is not that surprising.

Norman Swan: And people obviously with palliative chemotherapy.

Darren Saunders: People with palliative did worse. And there was some grainy
differences between the different hospitals.

Norman Swan: And there were differences between the hospitals which people
should take note of. So how was it reported?

Darren Saunders: The two main reports, one was in the Telegraph in the UK,
one was in the Guardian, and both got picked up on social media.
The Telegraph splashed with…their lead paragraph was all about chemotherapy
killing half the patients that get it. And that's…not anywhere in the paper does it
say that. And I've been through the press releases that went with it and nowhere
in those press releases do they say that.

Norman Swan: Okay, I guess it's a good headline.

Darren Saunders: Yes, and that got, as you could imagine, amplified massively
on social media, and I saw some really disturbing responses from patients and
patients' families saying, well, that's convinced me, I've told my doctor I don't
want therapy. The study didn't compare how people went with or without therapy,
so people are making big decisions based on this reporting here.

Norman Swan: And the Guardian?

Darren Saunders: The Guardian got it better, they actually pretty much covered
the story well. It was less sensationalist. They made some important points, but
they did it much better.

Norman Swan: And the argument here of course is because it goes out on
social media it washes against our shores as well. So was there much evidence
that it washed against our shores?

Darren Saunders: It did, it was widely reported even by some science and
health reporters within Australia on social media unfortunately.

Norman Swan: Picking up on the Telegraph headline rather than
the Guardian headline.

Darren Saunders: Yes, exactly, that was the headline that was quoted.

Norman Swan: So it's literally viral, it's infectious.

Darren Saunders: So it brings up this notion of…and forgive my language here,
this notion of the unbearable asymmetry of bullshit, as Brian Earp, the
philosopher in the UK has called it, and that's this notion that the amount of
energy necessary to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than it is to
produce it in the first place.

Norman Swan: How does this affect people like you who are cancer
researchers?

Darren Saunders: Frustration is the first word I'd use, it's incredibly frustrating.
It's hard enough getting accurate information out to people in the first place, and
when it's…I wouldn't say deliberately misrepresented but obviously not well
reported, it gets most of us pretty upset actually, to be honest.

Norman Swan: What's the poor punter to do? We had the Catalyst on statins
which reduced…some people would say cost 2,000 lives in Australia over a
period of time because people at high risk went off their statins. What is the poor
punter to do to actually work out what is a reliable article versus an unreliable
article?

Darren Saunders: It's really hard, especially when the by-line is science editor of
the Telegraph, that should be coming from a reputable voice. I guess I normally
point patients towards the National Institutes of Health in America or Cancer
Research UK or the Cancer Institute New South Wales who have reputable, well
collated information.

Norman Swan: So double-check before you decide that it's going to affect your
therapy.

Darren Saunders: Definitely.

Norman Swan: And this falls hard on the heels of bacon killing half the
population.

Darren Saunders: That was a great example…

Norman Swan: Cured meats and cancer.

Darren Saunders: Yes, the BBC reported that as being equally risky as
asbestos and plutonium, which it's clearly not.

Norman Swan: Yes, it smells too good for that! Darren, thanks for joining us.

Darren Saunders: Thanks Norman.

Norman Swan: Darren Saunders, who is in the department of pathology at the
University of New South Wales, and gnashing his teeth over cancer research
reporting.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on Radio National.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, depending on the state that you
live in, up to 50% of the population of Australia are functionally illiterate. A
proportion of these people will have dyslexia, but that's far from the only reason.
This Saturday, Learning Difficulties Australia's 2016 Eminent Researcher Award
is to be given to an old friend of the Health Report, Professor Maryanne Wolf,
who is director of the Centre for Reading and Language Research at Tufts
University in Boston, and she has dragged herself into the studio. Welcome back
Maryanne.

Maryanne Wolf: It's a pleasure to be back. Of course I have a multifactorial
response to give you and it's a developmental one, so pardon me if I give you
four different reasons at four different ages. The first is 0 to 5. We know that the
gaps really begin before the children even walk in the kindergarten door. So what
we could do to enhance language development is so simple, literally reading to
our children, speaking to our children every day, every night, is one of the
simplest antidotes to really the very grievous differences in language in our
privileged and underprivileged homes.

Norman Swan: So this is the notorious word gap.

Maryanne Wolf: This is the notorious word gap in which 32 million less words
are heard by children who are between three and four who come from
disadvantaged homes. And it's not just quantitative, it's qualitative as well, you
know, the nature of the language that is being used. But yes, that's the first, the 0
to 5.

Norman Swan: But if you've got 50% of the population, I think that's a
Tasmanian figure actually, I think it's less in other states, but if you've got a
large…even 30% is high, and their parents, they are going to struggle to read to
their children.

Maryanne Wolf: Absolutely. There are wonderful things that we can do, and part
of it is due to the paediatricians who are giving these various groups of children
stories that can be read either by the people who are the parents or by librarians
or by caretakers or by tape recorders…

Norman Swan: This is the US context.

Maryanne Wolf: This is the US context and it's called Reach Out and Read. But
any group can do this. So there's all kinds of ways we can do that. But actually I
think the more pernicious factor is happening between kindergarten and grades
two and three, and that's…and Norman, we've spoken about this before. I see a
certain recidivism going on in Australia in our methods of teaching children. So
regardless…

Norman Swan: So this is not the first time you've been to Australia?

Maryanne Wolf: This is definitely not the first time, I've even spoken to you
Norman about things that will make people very upset, and that is the nature of
instruction that goes on to children who come from whatever home they are…

Norman Swan: So this is before we even get on to dyslexia.

Maryanne Wolf: Oh, well before.

Norman Swan: And what you're talking about here is teachers training colleges
not teaching teachers evidence-based literacy.

Maryanne Wolf: Exactly. What I really was…I was so hopeful about Australia but
I see a retreat to binary modes of instruction…

Norman Swan: So what do you see happening?

Maryanne Wolf: I see instead of us really reflecting the research on evidence-
based instruction and the…

Norman Swan: And I should say there are like 30 randomised control trials of
this, this is not…

Maryanne Wolf: Yes, this is nothing new.

Norman Swan: And what we're talking about here, just to cut to the chase, is the
evidence-based teaching is phonics, sounding out words, understanding the
science within words and relating them to the written text, amongst other things.

Maryanne Wolf: Okay, amongst other things. But the way that I want the whole
public to understand this is that phonics provides the first scaffolding of a reading
brain circuitry. But by no means do people who have all the good intent in the
world in teaching whole language, we don't leave them behind, we provide that
scaffolding and expand it…

Norman Swan: And for those people who are listening to this for the first time,
whole language is the notion that there is something natural about reading. Your
point is that it's very unnatural to learn, that we didn't evolve to read. And they
think just by showing text and telling nice stories, kids will get it. And some kids
will, but not all.

Maryanne Wolf: Yes, right. Between 50% and 60% any method works, but for
the rest of our children we are literally not giving them the lower rungs of the
ladder. So they will never in fact reach their potential as truly expert readers
because of this.

Norman Swan: I'm used to hammering doctors for not being evidence-based,
now we are hammering teachers. What evidence have you got that there is
recidivism amongst Australian teachers and they are contributing to this
unacceptably high level of illiteracy?

Maryanne Wolf: What I have been doing for the last week but also for the last
several months is really trying to understand from teachers, policymakers,
administrators, what is going on, and what seems to be is a regression to a kind
of binary way of thinking about instruction.

Norman Swan: Binary?

Maryanne Wolf: Binary being phonics versus whole language and we can call it
balance but it's not balance. And what we really need to do is to understand
evidence base gives us a scaffolding. It also helps all children who have various
forms of impairments. So dyslexia is between 5% and 10% of the population.
There are many other challenges. But if you give this scaffolding and then you
expand it…you see, the reading brain circuit is not simply about phonics, that's
the beginning. I need teachers to realise they need to be explicit about everything
over time. So we are talking about rich semantic or vocabulary work…

Norman Swan: So it's understanding the world and the context for the written
word…

Maryanne Wolf: Exactly, syntax, the grammar, there's so much that is beautiful
about this reading brain circuit that is literally being taught in one way or another
versus a developmental sequenced way of bringing it all together.

Norman Swan: So do you think primary school teachers understand that syntax
and the grammar?

Maryanne Wolf: No, they do not. One of the really harsh realities is that primary
teachers are given the responsibility for all the ills the society is not addressing.

They are given 20, 25 or 30 children, they were never trained to work with
children with dyslexia or challenges, and they are giving usually one hour a week
from someone outside and no pull-out time for the children who need intensive
work.

Norman Swan: We're going to run out of time, so very briefly, looking at the 5%
of kids with dyslexia…

Maryanne Wolf: 5% to 10%, yes.

Norman Swan: I've been on a campaign about this with teachers, training
colleges, and obviously failed miserably. All we can do is talk about it. But I'm not
talking about the 5% who've got dyslexia and really something neurological going
on in their brain, what is new there in terms of being able to help them?

Maryanne Wolf: One of the most exciting aspects of all this work in
neuroscience is that we understand that our previous conceptualisation of
dyslexia was all wrong. It's not about a deficit or a defect, it's about a difference
in the brain organisation of those children. The educational system has not
understood that it is not the child, it's us. We can learn to teach this by
understanding how the reading brain circuit works and addressing each
component. That takes training. But we have evidence trials right now going on
from NICHD, we have wonderful methods that can with intensive pull-out training,
small group, we can do so much good, and release the potential of some of our
most creative minds who are dyslexic.

Norman Swan: So is handing an iPad to a baby changing the reading pathway?

Maryanne Wolf: Goodness gracious, the iPad is the new pacifier with the same
problems…

Norman Swan: Seriously, is the digital world changing how…?

Maryanne Wolf: The fourth factor I would say in functional illiteracy is the fact
that the digital world is in fact changing attention, especially in the young brain,
which is very susceptible. So you have addiction problems, you have children
who are literally developing a reading brain circuit that is short circuited, that

doesn't have the advantages because it's moving its attention sometimes 27
times an hour, they are not developing concentration…

Norman Swan: So you're talking about video-based material with rapid
intercutting.

Maryanne Wolf: But there's so many aspects to the digital culture that are
changing us. They are changing attention, memory, reliance on external
platforms of knowledge rather than building inside the children an internal…

Norman Swan: Most parents would think they are giving their children this
deeper knowledge and exposure to the world through the digital environment.
What is a parent to do?

Maryanne Wolf: First of all there's some wonderful work done by different
people, and what I would really suggest is that we have a developmental model.
Under two, I want no iPads. Between two and five, very gradual. At 5 to 7 I want
only use of the digital work in school for coding and programming. And then over
time, then we gradually use it, ever gradually.

Norman Swan: So it's not a tool for learning to read?

Maryanne Wolf: It is a tool that could be used carefully and critically. Literally we
need scales of justice here Norman, and in one minute I'm not going to be able to
say this but I will say that what I hope is a bi-literate brain that is critically able to
use and know when to use a digital reading and when to use print at what
developmental period. So it's a bi-literate brain over time developmentally taught.

Norman Swan: And Maryanne Wolf has got a couple of books coming out on
that which we will no doubt promote when they do. Maryanne, thanks very much
for joining us again on the Health Report.

Maryanne Wolf: Of course!

Norman Swan: Maryanne Wolf is director of the Centre for Reading and
Language Research at Tufts University in Boston.

I'm Norman Swan and you've been listening to the Health Report. I do hope you
can join us again next week
